details:
**Sukarno and Suharto**
Indonesia's first two presidents and the most common giveaways. Sukarno led the independence struggle against the Dutch and ruled from 1945 until he was pushed aside in 1966–67 by General Suharto, who ruled as an authoritarian until 1998 and reportedly embezzled as much as $15–35 billion.

**30 September Movement (1965)**
A failed coup attempt in which six army generals were kidnapped and killed in Jakarta. Suharto crushed it, blamed the communist PKI, and used it to sideline Sukarno; the event was later commemorated by a violent propaganda film broadcast every September 30.

**PKI and the 1965–66 mass killings**
The Communist Party of Indonesia, once one of the largest communist parties in the world. After the 30 September Movement, the army and allied militias killed roughly half a million or more suspected communists, an episode Vincent Bevins linked to later CIA-backed anti-leftist violence in his book The Jakarta Method.

**"Guided Democracy"**
Sukarno's authoritarian system, in place from 1957/59 to 1966, which replaced parliamentary democracy with rule balanced between the army, nationalists, religious groups, and the PKI. It caused a rift with his vice president Mohammad Hatta, who resigned in 1956.

**"New Order" (Orde Baru)**
Suharto's anti-communist, military-backed regime (1966–1998), which replaced Guided Democracy. Suharto was given emergency powers by the Supersemar order of March 11, 1966, and his economic policy was shaped by U.S.-trained technocrats nicknamed the "Berkeley Mafia."

**Bandung Conference (1955)**
A meeting of 29 Asian and African nations hosted by Sukarno in Bandung, attended by leaders like Zhou Enlai and Jawaharlal Nehru. It is considered the forerunner of the Non-Aligned Movement; Sukarno later tried to organize a "Conference of the New Emerging Forces."

**East Timor invasion and the Santa Cruz massacre**
Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 (Operation Seroja, "Lotus") to crush the FRETILIN independence movement and occupied it until 1999; it became independent in 2002. In the 1991 Santa Cruz massacre in Dili, troops shot pro-independence mourners in a cemetery, an event filmed by Max Stahl and witnessed by journalist Amy Goodman, who was beaten by soldiers.

**Batavia and the Dutch East India Company (VOC)**
The VOC founded Batavia (modern Jakarta) as its Asian headquarters in 1619 to control the spice trade; the colony was later called the Dutch East Indies. Colonial policies included the 1830 Culture System (forced cultivation of export crops on a share of village land) and the early-1900s "Ethical Policy" aimed at native welfare.

**Pancasila**
Indonesia's state ideology of "five principles" (belief in God, humanitarianism, national unity, democracy, and social justice), first articulated by Sukarno in 1945 and heavily enforced under Suharto. It is symbolized by the mythical bird Garuda on the national emblem, which carries the motto "Bhinneka Tunggal Ika" ("Unity in Diversity").

**Mohammad Hatta and the independence war**
Hatta and Sukarno proclaimed independence on August 17, 1945, just after the Japanese occupation ended. The Dutch tried to retake the colony in "police actions" such as Operation Product, the Linggadjati and Renville agreements set temporary terms, and the U.S. threatened Marshall Plan aid after the Dutch seized the revolutionary capital Yogyakarta; the Netherlands recognized independence in 1949.

**Majapahit Empire, Gajah Mada, and Hayam Wuruk**
A Hindu-Buddhist empire based on Java, founded by Raden Wijaya after the Singhasari kingdom's era and the defeat of a Mongol expedition in 1293. It peaked in the 14th century under King Hayam Wuruk and his prime minister Gajah Mada, who swore the Sumpah Palapa oath to abstain from spices until he unified the archipelago.

**Borobudur**
The world's largest Buddhist temple, in central Java, built by the Sailendra dynasty in the 8th–9th centuries. Its three levels represent the realms of desire (Kamadhatu), form (Rupadhatu), and formlessness (Arupadhatu).

**Konfrontasi and "To hell with your aid!"**
Sukarno's 1963–66 undeclared conflict opposing the formation of Malaysia, fought largely on Borneo against British Commonwealth forces. During this period Sukarno told the U.S. "To hell with your aid!" and withdrew Indonesia from the United Nations in 1965.

**Benedict Anderson's "Cornell Paper"**
A 1966 analysis by Cornell scholars Benedict Anderson and Ruth McVey that challenged the army's official account blaming the PKI for the 30 September Movement. Anderson was banned from entering Indonesia until 1999 as a result.

**Largest Muslim population and Aceh**
Indonesia has the world's largest Muslim population, with Islam spreading after the decline of the Srivijaya empire. Aceh, on the northern tip of Sumatra, observes sharia law; Javanese Islam is divided between pious santri and syncretic abangan, and the reformist Muhammadiyah is a major organization.
